newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr under intense pressure,1996 low at risk.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr under intense pressure,1996 low at risk.

text.p: The Australian dollar came under intense pressure Wednesday, losing 1/3 cent cent and threatening to violate vital support at the 1996 low of US$0.7305.
Traders said U.S. and Swiss banks had led a sustained selling attack all morning, with at least A$400-A$500 million estimated to have been dumped so far swamping some good bids.

The driving force remained fear the Reserve Bank would cut interest rates again, the fifth move this cycle, but there were plenty of other reasons to be bearish ranging from technicals to commodity prices, negative reports by U.S. investment banks and talk of a U.K. company taking billions of sale proceeds home.
By 12.00 pm (0200 GMT) the dollar had extended an offshore rout to cower at US$0.7315/20 having started at US$0.7345/50 from US$0.7360/65 late here Tuesday.

This was the fifth successive session of fresh 18-month lows and brought the losses suffered since Friday's local close to 1-1/3 cents and to almost six percent since the Reserve Bank caught the market unawares with its last rate easing on May 23. The latter event had seen domestic money rates sink below those in the U.S. -- a situation virtually without precedent and one not to the taste of offshore investors used to thinking of the A$ as a high yielder -- in expectation of yet another cut.
The dollar had entered a major bear trend in response and was now in danger of breaching the US$0.7305 low which would take it to territory not visited since August 1995.
Analysts saw some support around US$0.7290 and US$0.7250 but felt the momentum of the downtrend was such that a return to the 1995 trough at US$0.7070 was now a real prospect.
Among the many reasons to be bearish was the latest weekly currency report from Goldman Sachs in which it re-stated its long-standing recommendation to sell the Australian dollar.
The U.S. investment bank had a three-month target of 73 cents but said a fall below 70 cents could not be ruled out.
Traders said the warning was no surprise since Goldman, along with a who's who of other investment houses, had been a persistent seller of the currency in recent weeks.

The Goldman report was equally downbeat on the New Zealand dollar saying the Kiwi would not be fair value until it hit 60 U.S. cents. The Kiwi was down sharply at US$0.6573/80 today from US$0.6648/58 late Tuesday. The A$ had the better of the exchange here and edged higher to NZ$1.1125/44 from NZ$1.1056/72.
The local dollar was also troubled by talk U.K. company ICI was repatriating funds from the sale of its 62.4 percent holding in ICI Australia, the term sof which were finalised last week.
The sale of the shares, some of which were bought by ICI Australia and some offered through a global issue, was estimated to have netted the British company around A$2.2 billion.

Commodity prices had been another negative recently with the influential Commodity Research Bureau index plumbing two year lows at 232.01 last week. It had steadied somewhat since with a bounce to 235.15, but remained short of former pivotal support at 236.00 and some key Australian commodities like gold, copper and wheat remained in downtrends.
If this were not bearish enough, there was now a risk many more exports could be hit by industrial strife.
Front page newspaper reports claimed a five week old dispute at a New South Wales coal mine could escalate into a national strike at mines and ports.
The threat seemed to lessen somewhat this morning, however, when the main union involved said it was seeking to start negotiations with the company in the Industrial Relations Commission on Thursday.
On the crosses the local currency found some support from a firmer US$/yen and rose to 84.56/66 yen from 84.00/10 but still eased to 56.4 on its trade weighted index from 56.5.
